title: Coupled Cluster con MoLe: Molecular Orbital Learning for Neural Wavefunctions
claim: A structured input is transformed through staged encoding, alternating message-passing and attention modules, and a final readout that directly outputs the target quantities.
layout: Two rows of boxes, left-to-right then wrapping down; labeled arrows, stacked-layer motifs
description: A two-row pipeline diagram. The top row starts with a water-like molecule (XYZ) in a rounded gray box. An arrow labeled HF leads to a grid of molecular-orbital coefficients C, colored in red, blue and light-blue row blocks, with small molecule thumbnails and an ellipsis below it. An arrow labeled pad leads to a padded version of the grid, and an arrow labeled embed leads to a stacked card of graph states, where each atom carries a vertical bar of coefficients. A long black arrow wraps to the bottom row. There, stacked Message Passing cards with curved colored arrows between atoms alternate with tall gray Attention slabs, twice, separated by dots. The output splits into two readouts: a small o-by-v tensor and a larger ov-by-ov pink-purple matrix. Heavy black arrows guide the eye from the top left.
caption: Given a molecule, a Hartree-Fock calculation provides the molecular orbitals represented by their coefficient matrix C. The coefficient vector is padded for each atom to ensure that they all have the same number of basis coefficients, enabling their embedding in an equivariant neural network. The model then alternates message passing to mix information within the MOs and attention layers to mix information between MOs. Finally, the embeddings are read out by “outer product-like” operations, outputting the T1 and T2 amplitudes.
abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) is the most widely used method for calculating molecular properties; however, its accuracy is often insufficient for quantitative predictions. Coupled-cluster (CC) theory is the most successful method for achieving accuracy beyond DFT and for predicting properties that closely align with experiment. It is known as the ''gold standard'' of quantum chemistry. Unfortunately, the high computational cost of CC limits its widespread applicability. In this work, we present the Molecular Orbital Learning (MÅLe) architecture, an equivariant machine learning model that directly predicts CC's core mathematical objects, the excitation amplitudes, from the mean-field Hartree-Fock molecular orbitals as inputs. We test various aspects of our model and demonstrate its remarkable data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization to larger molecules and off-equilibrium geometries, despite being trained only on small equilibrium geometries. Finally, we also examine its ability to reduce the number of cycles required to converge CC calculations. MÅLe can set the foundations for high-accuracy wavefunction-based ML architectures to accelerate molecular design and complement force-field approaches.
